edges.description: Chronic IL-6-driven inflammation is associated with large-artery and small-vessel ischemic stroke, plausibly through atherosclerosis and small-vessel disease. The causal link rests on genetic evidence, and anti-inflammatory treatment has not yet been shown to prevent recurrence.
In ageing, the bone-marrow response to stroke produces atypical, pro-oxidant and procoagulant neutrophils that plug the ischemic microcirculation and worsen injury.
Occlusion creates a severely hypoperfused core and a potentially salvageable penumbra with residual perfusion.
Energy failure and the return of oxygen at reperfusion load neuronal mitochondria with calcium and reactive oxygen species.
Energy failure disrupts ionic gradients and glutamate handling, triggering calcium overload, oxidative injury, and cell death.
Ischemic injury activates vascular, glial, and immune responses in the neurovascular unit.
Energy failure activates macroautophagy within hours of occlusion, with autophagosome numbers and autophagy-marker levels in the ischemic penumbra rising over the following days.
Astrocytes and cerebral endothelial cells within the ischemic territory undergo acute cellular senescence following arterial occlusion.

edges.description: Mitochondrial ROS generation and permeability transition contribute to the oxidative and apoptotic-like neuronal death modeled in that node. Persistent mitochondrial failure is not required for infarction after shorter ischemia.

nodes.description: Middle cerebral artery occlusion triggers acute cellular senescence in astrocytes and cerebral endothelial cells within the ischemic hemisphere, marked by p16INK4a upregulation and a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) of MMP-3, IL-1alpha, and IL-6. Senolytic clearance of these senescent cells, whether systemic (ABT-263) or local (targeted lenti-INK-ATTAC), reduces SASP factor levels and improves neurological and locomotor outcomes after occlusion. A senescence-associated blood gene-expression signature is independently associated with worse 90-day functional outcome in acute ischemic stroke patients.

nodes.description: Persistently raised circulating inflammatory markers, chiefly interleukin-6 and C-reactive protein, mark a higher risk of a first ischemic stroke and of recurrence after one. Genetic evidence that lower IL-6 signaling lowers the risk of large-artery and small-vessel stroke, but not cardioembolic stroke, suggests the IL-6 axis is causal rather than only a marker. In aged mice, age-related changes in blood-cell production generate atypical neutrophils that worsen the inflammatory response to stroke, and related neutrophil subsets track with worse reperfusion in elderly patients. Most of the human evidence concerns inflammation in general rather than inflammation driven by ageing, so this node is a disease-specific use of the inflammaging module. Anti-inflammatory treatment has not yet been shown to prevent stroke: low-dose colchicine did not reduce early recurrence in a large trial.

nodes.description: Macroautophagy is activated within the ischemic penumbra after arterial occlusion, with autophagosome numbers and autophagy-marker (Beclin-1, LC3B) levels rising early and then declining over the following days as autophagic flux weakens. In parallel, the lysosomal protease cathepsin D (CTSD) is progressively lost, and this lysosomal dysfunction, rather than autophagy induction itself, is the step this node conforms to: loss of CTSD is sufficient to cause lysosomal dysfunction and aggravates neuronal death under oxygen-glucose deprivation, while restoring CTSD activity protects neurons.

nodes.description: After arterial occlusion and reperfusion, neuronal mitochondria generate reactive oxygen species and open the permeability transition pore, which couples the energy failure of the penumbra to neuronal death. In rodent focal ischemia, mitochondria in the ischemic focus lose respiratory capacity, and succinate that accumulates during ischemia is re-oxidized on reperfusion, driving the reactive oxygen species burst by reverse electron transport at complex I. This is an acute injury process, not the age-related decline the conformed module describes; the shared element is the bioenergetic-failure and oxidative-stress state. Mechanistic support is almost entirely from rodents, and the one randomized human test of targeting the pore (cyclosporine) missed its primary endpoint, so the causal weight of this node in human stroke is unsettled.
